Its total cooling energy consumption (including cooling and cooling fans/pumps) was reduced from 46.5 MBtu to 38.6 MBtu, representing a 17% reduction. Because heating demand in Hawai‘i is negligible, heating savings are not analyzed for this location. The example dwelling unit in North Carolina (climate zone 3A) also uses electricity for both heating and cooling. Its cooling energy consumption was reduced from 11.3 MBtu to 9.0 MBtu, a 20% reduction. Additionally, total heating energy consumption (heating, heating fan/pumps, heat pump backup, and associated fans/pumps) was reduced from 19.7 MBtu to 14.7 MBtu, a 25% reduction. The example dwelling unit in Alaska (climate zone 8AK) uses fuel oil for heating and has no cooling system; therefore, cooling savings are not analyzed for this location. Its total heating energy use (heating and heating fans/pumps) was reduced from 167 MBtu to 135.7 MBtu, representing a 19% reduction. 7 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. The percentage reduction in energy use for these three example dwelling units is similar to findings from a field study conducted by Jump et al. (1996). In that study, 24 houses in the Sacramento, California, area were tested before and after duct retrofitting. The average air leakage was reduced from 18% to 9% after the retrofit, resulting in an average 18% decrease in HVAC energy use (Jump, Walker, & Modera, 1996). Figure 1. January 2 is selected to examine the heating time-series data, while July 2 is selected to examine the cooling time-series data.
